title: Blackout Wednesday: A Safe Plan for the Night Before Thanksgiving
excerpt: Blackout Wednesday is the night before Thanksgiving. How to enjoy it without blacking out: a ride-home plan, pacing, alcohol poisoning signs, and next-day recovery.
metaDescription: Blackout Wednesday, the night before Thanksgiving: how to avoid blacking out, get home safe, spot alcohol poisoning, and recover for Thanksgiving dinner.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Blackout Wednesday is the nickname for the night before Thanksgiving, when people home for the holiday pack into hometown bars and house parties and drink more than they usually would. The name is a joke, but the risks are real: the Thanksgiving travel period is one of the most dangerous times of year on US roads for alcohol-impaired crashes, and fast, heavy drinking is exactly what causes memory blackouts. You can still have a great night with old friends. The trick is to make three decisions before you go out, while you are sober: how you are getting home, roughly how much you will drink, and what you will eat first. This guide gives you a simple plan for the night, how to spot an emergency, and how to be functional for Thanksgiving dinner.

> **Get a ride home. Decide it now.** Before you leave the house, settle exactly how you are getting home: a sober friend who has agreed to drive, a rideshare app already set up with your payment card, a taxi number saved in your phone, or a couch at the house where the party is. Do not plan to "see how you feel." Alcohol impairs judgment before you notice it, and the person least able to judge whether you can drive is you after a few drinks. Driving the next morning can also be unsafe if you drank late and heavily. If someone in your group is too drunk to get home safely, make sure they get a ride too.

> **When to get help right away.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone** cannot be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute, or long gaps between breaths), has a seizure, has blue, gray, or very pale skin or lips, feels cold and clammy, or is vomiting while drowsy or confused. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, which can kill. Do not wait for every sign to appear, and do not leave the person alone to "sleep it off." In the US you can also call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** for advice. If you take any prescription medicine, talk to your doctor or pharmacist about how it interacts with alcohol before a big night out.

## What Is Blackout Wednesday?

Blackout Wednesday (also called Drinksgiving, Black Wednesday, or simply Thanksgiving Eve) is the Wednesday night before American Thanksgiving. Bar owners and news outlets regularly describe it as one of the busiest bar nights of the year, often mentioned in the same breath as New Year's Eve and St. Patrick's Day.

A few things line up to make it a big night:

- **Almost everyone has Thursday off.** For many people it's the first night in months with no work or class the next morning.
- **Everyone is back home at once.** College students, young adults who moved away, and old school friends all land in the same town on the same day. The hometown bar becomes a reunion.
- **Holiday stress.** Travel, family dynamics, and a big day of hosting or visiting coming up can make a drink or five feel like a release.
- **It's a tradition.** When a night has a nickname with "blackout" in it, it nudges people toward drinking like the name suggests.

None of that is a problem on its own. Catching up with people you haven't seen in a year is one of the best parts of the holiday. The trouble comes from the combination: a crowded bar, rounds being bought for big groups, shots to celebrate, a long gap since dinner, and a drive home in a town where public transit is thin and everyone parked at the bar.

## What Actually Happens in a Blackout

The name refers to an alcohol-induced blackout, which is a gap in memory for things that happened while you were drinking. You were awake, walking, and talking, but your brain was not recording it properly.

Here is the plain version of the science. A part of the brain called the **hippocampus** is responsible for turning what's happening right now into memories you can recall later. Alcohol interferes with the signaling the hippocampus uses to do that. At high enough levels it can largely stop new memories from forming, even though you can still hold a conversation in the moment. Researchers at the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) have written extensively on this.

There are two kinds:

- **A fragmentary blackout ("brownout")** is patchy. You remember bits of the night, and sometimes a reminder brings a piece back.
- **An en bloc blackout** is a complete gap. A whole stretch of time is simply missing, and no reminder brings it back.

### Why speed matters more than the total

The most useful thing to know about blackouts is that they are strongly linked to **how fast your blood alcohol level rises**, not only how much you drink in total. Research on blackouts consistently points to rapid drinking, drinking on an empty stomach, and shots or strong drinks taken quickly as the main triggers. That is exactly the pattern a crowded Thanksgiving Eve bar encourages: someone buys a round of shots, then another, before dinner has even been digested.

This is also why a blackout is a warning sign and not a funny story. If you drank enough to stop forming memories, you were also drinking enough to seriously impair your balance, judgment, and reaction time. During a blackout people can make decisions that are completely out of character, including getting behind the wheel, getting into fights, or leaving with someone they wouldn't otherwise go with. You will not remember those decisions, but they still happened.

## The Real Risks on Thanksgiving Eve

Most people who go out on Blackout Wednesday come home fine, wake up a bit rough, and eat too much turkey. It's still worth being clear about the things that go wrong, because most of them are preventable with a little planning.

**Drunk driving.** This is the big one. The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and groups like Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD) run campaigns around the Thanksgiving holiday every year because the long weekend combines heavy travel with heavy drinking. Many hometowns have limited late-night transit, so people drive to the bar and then face a choice at closing time. Police departments in many areas also increase patrols and sobriety checkpoints that night. In every US state the legal limit for adult drivers is a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) of 0.08%, and Utah's is lower at 0.05%. But impairment starts well below the legal limit.

**Alcohol poisoning.** When someone drinks a large amount quickly, their blood alcohol can keep rising even after they stop, because alcohol still in the stomach and gut keeps being absorbed. That's why a friend who "only" passed out can get worse over the next hour. Alcohol poisoning slows the parts of the brain that control breathing, heart rate, and body temperature, and it can stop the gag reflex, which means a person can choke on their own vomit.

**Injuries and falls.** Icy sidewalks in late November, unfamiliar stairs at a house party, and poor balance are a bad mix.

**Cold exposure.** Alcohol makes you feel warm because it widens blood vessels near the skin, but that actually makes your body lose heat faster. Walking home drunk in the cold, or falling asleep outside, is dangerous.

**Medication interactions.** If you take anything that makes you drowsy (sleep aids, anxiety medicines, some antidepressants, opioid painkillers, antihistamines, muscle relaxers), alcohol can multiply that effect. Ask a pharmacist before a heavy night.

**The next day.** A bad hangover, or still being over the limit at 10 a.m. when you're supposed to drive to grandma's, can affect the actual holiday.

## Your Blackout Wednesday Game Plan

You don't need a spreadsheet. You need a handful of decisions made while you're still sober, because those are the ones that hold up at midnight.

### Before you go out

1. **Lock in your ride home.** Pick one: a designated driver who has agreed not to drink at all, a rideshare or taxi, a walkable route, or a place to sleep. Set up the rideshare app and your payment card before you leave, so it's one tap later. If you're driving to meet people, consider leaving the car at home entirely so the choice is made for you.
2. **Eat a real meal.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which flattens the spike that causes blackouts. A meal with protein, fat, and some carbs a couple of hours before is ideal. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers what helps most. A handful of chips at 11 p.m. doesn't count.
3. **Pick a rough number.** Decide in advance roughly how many drinks you're having. It doesn't have to be low. It has to exist, because "I'll just see" usually means you lose count after the third round.
4. **Charge your phone and share your location** with a friend or family member. If you get separated from your group, someone can find you.
5. **Know what's in your system.** If you're on a prescription, check the label or ask a pharmacist about alcohol now, not at the bar.

### At the bar or party

- **Pace by the clock.** Your body clears alcohol at roughly one standard drink per hour, and you can't speed that up. Drinking faster than that means your blood alcohol keeps climbing. Aiming for no more than one drink an hour keeps the rise gentle.
- **Know what a "drink" is.** In the US, one standard drink is about 14 grams of pure alcohol: a 12-ounce beer at 5% alcohol, a 5-ounce glass of wine at about 12%, or a 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof liquor. A pint of strong craft IPA, a heavy-pour cocktail, or a double can be two or more standard drinks in one glass.
- **Alternate with water.** Have a glass of water or soda between alcoholic drinks. It slows your pace without anyone noticing, and it helps with the dehydration side of tomorrow's hangover.
- **Go easy on shots and rounds.** Shots are the fastest way to spike your blood alcohol, and group rounds mean you drink on the group's schedule, not yours. It's fine to say "I'm good, I've got one" and hold up your drink. Nobody tracks it as closely as you think.
- **Watch the drinks you didn't pour.** Punch bowls, jungle juice, and "mystery" mixed drinks at house parties can contain far more alcohol than they taste like. Sweet mixers hide strong liquor well.
- **Keep an eye on your drink.** Don't leave it unattended, and don't accept one you didn't see poured.
- **Eat again late.** If the night runs long, a late snack or bar food helps.
- **Stick with your people.** Agree with your friends that nobody leaves alone and nobody leaves without telling the group.

### Heading home

- **Use the ride you planned.** This is the moment the earlier decision pays off. Don't reopen the question.
- **Don't let a friend drive drunk.** Take their keys if you can, get them a ride, or have them stay over. It's an awkward minute that can prevent the worst night of their life.
- **Before bed, drink water and eat something light.** A glass or two of water and some toast won't sober you up, but it can make the morning a little easier.
- **Skip the "just in case" painkillers.** Don't take acetaminophen (Tylenol) before bed after drinking. If you wake up with a headache, deal with it then, after you've eaten.

## How to Avoid Blacking Out

Since blackouts are mostly about how fast your blood alcohol climbs, the practical advice is about slowing the climb:

- **Never drink on an empty stomach.** This is the single biggest lever you control.
- **Avoid shots, especially back-to-back.** If you do one to join a toast, follow it with water and give it time.
- **Sip, don't gulp.** Choose drinks you naturally drink slowly, like a beer or a glass of wine, over a strong cocktail you finish in five minutes.
- **Count honestly.** Count standard drinks, not glasses.
- **Be careful with other substances.** Mixing alcohol with sedating medicines or other drugs makes blackouts and dangerous sedation much more likely.
- **Notice the early warning.** If you realize you can't remember how you got from one place to another, or a friend has to repeat something they just told you, stop drinking alcohol for the night. Switch to water and food, and tell a friend.

People who have had a blackout before are more likely to have another, so if this has happened to you on past Thanksgiving Eves, plan more conservatively this year.

## Signs of Alcohol Poisoning: How to Tell a Drunk Friend From an Emergency

Lots of people get very drunk on Thanksgiving Eve. Most need water, food, and a ride home. Some need an ambulance. The difference matters, and it's easy to get wrong when everyone around you has been drinking too.

**Call 911 if a person has any of these:**

- Can't be woken up, or can't stay awake
- Slow breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or irregular breathing with gaps of 10 seconds or more
- Seizures
- Blue, gray, or very pale skin, lips, or fingernails
- Low body temperature, feeling cold and clammy
- Vomiting while confused or barely conscious
- Severe confusion, or not responding normally to you

The NIAAA and the CDC list these same warning signs. You don't need all of them, and you don't need to be sure. If you're unsure, call.

**While you wait for help:**

- **Stay with them.** Don't leave them alone to sleep it off.
- **Turn them onto their side** (the recovery position) with their head tilted slightly, so if they vomit it drains out rather than going into their lungs.
- **Keep them warm** with a blanket or coat.
- **Don't give them coffee or a cold shower.** Neither sobers anyone up, and a cold shower can make low body temperature worse.
- **Don't make them walk it off,** and don't give them more alcohol.
- **Tell the paramedics what they drank and whether they took any medicine or drugs.** That information helps them treat the person.

Many US states have Good Samaritan or medical amnesty laws designed so that people who call for help in an alcohol or drug emergency are protected from certain penalties, including some underage drinking charges. The details vary by state, but the principle is the same everywhere: getting someone medical help is always the right call.

## Thanksgiving Morning: Can You Drive?

This catches a lot of people out. If you were drinking until 1 or 2 a.m., you may still have alcohol in your blood when you wake up, especially after a heavy night. Sleep doesn't speed up how your body clears alcohol, and neither do coffee, a shower, or a big breakfast. Your liver works through it at roughly one standard drink per hour no matter what you do.

A rough way to think about it: if you finished your last drink at 2 a.m. after ten standard drinks, it can easily take until late morning or later before your blood alcohol is back to zero. Everyone's body is different, so you can't calculate this precisely in your head. If you had a big night and feel even slightly off, let someone else drive to the family meal, or leave later. Feeling hungover also impairs driving on its own, even after the alcohol has cleared, because of tiredness, slower reactions, and poor concentration.

## Surviving Thanksgiving Day With a Hangover

You've got a turkey to baste or a long table of relatives to make conversation with. Here's what helps:

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Alcohol makes you pee more, so you start the day short on fluid. Sip water through the morning instead of chugging a liter at once. If you've been sick or sweaty, an electrolyte drink can help. Our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) explains when it makes a difference.
- **Eat something simple early.** Toast, eggs, bananas, or oatmeal are easy on an unsettled stomach and help bring your blood sugar back up. Don't save all your appetite for the big meal.
- **Pick your painkiller carefully.** If you need one, ibuprofen or naproxen with food is usually gentler on the liver than acetaminophen after drinking, but harder on the stomach. If you have stomach, kidney, or liver problems, or take blood thinners, ask a pharmacist. Follow the label either way.
- **Skip "hair of the dog."** A mimosa at brunch may dull the hangover for an hour, but it mostly just delays it, and you're stacking more alcohol on a body that's still recovering. It also makes the afternoon drinks hit harder.
- **Get some fresh air and gentle movement.** A short walk can help you feel more human.
- **Pace the holiday drinks.** If there's wine with dinner, it's fine to have a glass, but go slowly and eat first. A second big drinking session in 24 hours is when hangovers get really ugly.
- **Nap if you can.** Alcohol wrecks sleep quality, so a short nap after the meal is legitimately useful.

### The turkey tryptophan myth

You'll hear that turkey makes you sleepy because of tryptophan. Turkey does contain tryptophan, but no more than many other common proteins like chicken or cheese. The post-dinner slump is more likely a mix of a huge meal, lots of carbs, wine at the table, and, if you went out the night before, a short and poor night's sleep. In other words, Blackout Wednesday may be doing more to put you to sleep on the couch than the turkey is.

For a broader plan for the whole season, including office parties and New Year's Eve, see our [holiday drinking survival guide](/never-hungover/holiday-drinking-survival-guide-health-first-approach).

## If You're Hosting or Looking Out for Others

If the Thanksgiving Eve party is at your place, or you're the friend who tends to look after everyone:

- **Put out real food,** not just snacks. People drink slower when they're eating.
- **Have plenty of water and non-alcoholic options** visible and easy to grab. A good non-alcoholic option makes it easy for the designated driver to stay sober.
- **Be careful with big-batch punch.** If you make one, don't load it with high-proof liquor, and tell people what's in it.
- **Offer couches and floor space.** Saying "anyone can crash here" early in the night removes the pressure to drive.
- **Collect keys if it makes sense** for your group.
- **Know who's leaving and how.** A quick "how are you getting home?" at the door goes a long way.

## Is It Just One Night? A Note for the Next Morning

For most people, Blackout Wednesday is one big night a year with old friends, and that's okay. Still, it's worth paying attention if any of these keep happening: you regularly drink much more than you planned, you've had several blackouts, people close to you have raised concerns, or you find yourself needing a drink to get through family events. None of that means anything dramatic about who you are. It's just useful information, and a doctor is a good, judgment-free place to talk it through. If you drink heavily every day and get shaky, sweaty, or very anxious when you stop, tell a doctor before cutting back suddenly, because stopping abruptly can be medically risky for people who drink that way.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people add a supplement like DHM (dihydromyricetin) to their routine on big nights. Here's an honest view.

DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree (Hovenia dulcis). A widely cited 2012 study in rats, published in the *Journal of Neuroscience*, found DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal in the animals. That's interesting early research, but it was in rats. Human data on hangovers is limited, and most of what's known comes from lab and animal studies.

What DHM is **not**:

- **It is not a way to sober up.** There is no good evidence that DHM lowers your blood alcohol level or makes it safe to drive. Only time does that.
- **It is not blackout protection.** There is no good evidence that DHM prevents blackouts or alcohol poisoning. The only reliable protection is drinking less and drinking slower.
- **It is not a reason to drink more.** If a supplement makes you feel comfortable having extra rounds, it's working against you.

If you want to try DHM as part of a sensible plan (food first, a pace you've chosen, water between drinks, and a ride home already booked), popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence. If you take prescription medicine, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Blackout Wednesday is the night before Thanksgiving, one of the biggest drinking nights of the year in the US because everyone is home and nobody works Thursday.
- Blackouts are mostly caused by blood alcohol rising fast, so eat a real meal, pace yourself at about one drink an hour, alternate with water, and go easy on shots.
- **Decide how you're getting home before you leave.** Never drive after drinking, and be careful about driving the next morning too.
- Know the signs of alcohol poisoning. If someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, or has a seizure, call 911 and keep them on their side.
- On Thanksgiving Day, hydrate, eat early, skip hair of the dog, and pace the wine at dinner.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is Blackout Wednesday?**

Blackout Wednesday is a nickname for the night before Thanksgiving in the US, also called Drinksgiving or Thanksgiving Eve. It's known as one of the busiest bar nights of the year because many people have Thursday off and are back in their hometowns reuniting with old friends. The name refers to drinking heavily enough to have memory blackouts, which is a sign of dangerously fast drinking, not a goal.

**Why is the night before Thanksgiving such a big drinking night?**

Several things line up at once. Most people have the next day off, college students and young adults who moved away are all back home on the same night, hometown bars turn into reunions, and holiday stress makes a night out feel like a release. Group rounds, shots, and long gaps since dinner then push people to drink faster than usual.

**How can I avoid blacking out on Blackout Wednesday?**

Blackouts are strongly linked to how fast your blood alcohol rises. Eat a real meal before you go out, aim for no more than about one standard drink an hour, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, and avoid back-to-back shots. If you notice gaps in your memory or a friend has to repeat things, stop drinking alcohol for the night and switch to water and food.

**What are the signs of alcohol poisoning?**

Call 911 if someone can't be woken up, is breathing slowly (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or irregularly, has a seizure, has blue, gray, or very pale skin or lips, feels cold and clammy, or is vomiting while confused or barely conscious. Stay with them, turn them onto their side so they can't choke, keep them warm, and don't give them coffee or a cold shower. You don't need to be certain before calling.

**Can I drive on Thanksgiving morning after drinking Wednesday night?**

Maybe not. If you drank heavily until late, you can still have alcohol in your blood the next morning, because your body clears it at roughly one standard drink per hour and sleep, coffee, and showers don't speed that up. A heavy hangover also impairs driving on its own. If you had a big night, let someone else drive or leave later.

**How do I get over a hangover in time for Thanksgiving dinner?**

Sip water steadily through the morning, add an electrolyte drink if you've been sick, and eat something simple early like toast, eggs, or a banana. If you need a painkiller, take it with food and follow the label. Skip hair of the dog, get some fresh air, nap if you can, and pace any wine at dinner so you're not stacking a second heavy session on top of the first.

**Does turkey make you sleepy, or is it the hangover?**

Turkey contains tryptophan, but no more than many other common proteins like chicken or cheese. The post-dinner slump is more likely from a huge meal, lots of carbs, wine at the table, and a short, poor night of sleep after drinking on Wednesday. Alcohol disrupts sleep quality, so a big night out can do more to make you drowsy on Thursday than the turkey does.

**Does DHM prevent blackouts or help you sober up?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents blackouts, lowers your blood alcohol, or makes it safe to drive. Only time clears alcohol from your body. DHM has interesting early research, mostly in animals, and some people use it as part of a hangover routine, but it's not a substitute for eating, pacing your drinks, and arranging a safe ride home.
